pos: n. (proper, a king of Assyria; Assyrian, Ashur has given a brother)
etymology: Assyrian Ashur-aha-iddina, Ashur has given a brother. Son of Sennacherib, he came to the throne over his father's murdered body, and the Authorized Version names him three times — twice in the same sentence recorded in two books, and once in the mouth of Judah's enemies.
biblical_def: Isaiah had prophesied that Sennacherib would return to his own land and fall by the sword there, and the fulfilment is recorded twice in identical words: “And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead” (2 Kings 19:37; Isaiah 37:38). The king who had mocked the God of Israel died at the feet of an idol that could not defend him, killed by his own sons, and Esarhaddon inherited the throne. His name surfaces again a century and a half later, when the adversaries of Judah offer to help rebuild the temple: “we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither” (Ezra 4:2). The mixed population he had settled in Samaria had a mixed religion, and Zerubbabel refused the offer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; the sense is fixed by Scripture, where Esarhaddon is the son of Sennacherib who reigned in his stead after his murder.
webster_full: ASSYRIA, n. An ancient kingdom of western Asia, whose capital was Nineveh, long the scourge and at last the captor of the northern kingdom of Israel.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
USURP, v.t. To seize and hold in possession by force or without right; as, to usurp a throne.
SAMARITAN, n. An inhabitant of Samaria; one of a people formed from the mingling of foreign colonists with the remnant of Israel.
SYNCRETISM, n. The attempted union of principles or parties irreconcilably at variance with each other.
scriptures: 2 Kings 19:37

And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword: and they escaped into the land of Armenia. And Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.
Isaiah 37:38

And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god, that Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons smote him with the sword; and they escaped into the land of Armenia: and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his stead.
Ezra 4:2

Then they came to Zerubbabel, and to the chief of the fathers, and said unto them, Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither.
Ezra 4:3

But Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and the rest of the chief of the fathers of Israel, said unto them, Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build unto the LORD God of Israel, as king Cyrus the king of Persia hath commanded us.
corruption_summary: Offers of religious partnership from those who sacrifice to the LORD alongside other gods are welcomed today as generous ecumenism; Zerubbabel refused exactly such an offer from the people Esarhaddon had settled.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 4 records one of the most instructive refusals in Scripture, and it is regularly judged narrow. The adversaries approach with warm words: Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye do; and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither. Everything about it sounds cooperative. 2 Kings 17 tells the reader what their religion actually was — they feared the LORD and served their own gods — and Zerubbabel answered that they had nothing to do with the house of God, but that Israel alone would build. A shared vocabulary about God is not a shared faith, and the test of partnership is the doctrine, not the warmth of the offer.

The other half of Esarhaddon's appearance is a lesson in how God answers blasphemy. Sennacherib had sent letters asking whether the God of Jerusalem could deliver better than the gods of Hamath and Arpad. Isaiah answered that he would return by the way he came and not shoot an arrow into the city, and he did. The end came not in battle but in a temple: the great king worshipping Nisroch, and his own sons behind him with swords. The God who is mocked does not always answer at once, and when he answers he frequently uses the mocker's own household.
roots_summary: Assyrian Ashur-aha-iddina, Ashur has given a brother; Hebrew Ecarchaddown (H634); Cancheriyb (H5576), Sennacherib; Nicrok (H5268), Nisroch.

Hebrew Cancheriyb (H5576) — Sennacherib, his father, slain while worshipping.
Hebrew Nicrok (H5268) — Nisroch, the god in whose house Sennacherib died.

“Since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur” — the offer Zerubbabel refused.
“Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God”.

pos: n. (proper, a city on the Euphrates)
etymology: Hebrew Karkemiysh, a fortress city commanding the chief crossing of the upper Euphrates. It appears three times in the Authorized Version, and each time it marks a hinge on which the history of nations turned.
biblical_def: Isaiah names it in the Assyrian's boast, as one of the cities that had fallen and proved that no city could stand: “Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?” (Isaiah 10:9). A century later it is the destination of the march that killed Josiah: “when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him” (2 Chronicles 35:20) — and Josiah, warned by Necho not to meddle, disguised himself, fought, and was shot at Megiddo. Then Jeremiah dates the collapse of Egypt to the same place: his oracle is “against the army of Pharaohnecho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah” (Jeremiah 46:2). One ford on one river, and the empire that ruled the world changed hands there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as a city upon the river Euphrates, the site of the battle in which Nebuchadrezzar smote the army of Pharaoh-necho.
webster_full: EUPHRATES, n. One of the great rivers of western Asia, rising in Armenia and flowing to the Persian gulf; a boundary of the promised land.
FORD, n. A place in a river or other water where it may be passed by man or beast on foot, or by wading.
EMPIRE, n. Supreme power in governing; imperial power; the territories subject to an emperor.
BATTLE, n. A fight or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.
OVERRULE, v.t. To influence or control by predominant power; to govern with high authority.
scriptures: Isaiah 10:9
Is not Calno as Carchemish? is not Hamath as Arpad? is not Samaria as Damascus?
2 Chronicles 35:20
After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates: and Josiah went out against him.
Jeremiah 46:2

Against Egypt, against the army of Pharaohnecho king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah.
2 Chronicles 35:22

Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo.
corruption_summary: World history is narrated as the product of armies and interests alone; Scripture attaches the same battles to God's purpose, and records that Josiah died because he would not hear a warning that came through a pagan king.
corruption_paragraphs: Carchemish is a fixed point in secular chronology, and the Bible treats it as a fixed point in the government of God. Isaiah has the Assyrian boasting of it and then declares that Assyria is the rod of God's anger, a tool that does not know whose hand holds it. Jeremiah dates Nebuchadrezzar's victory there to a regnal year of Jehoiakim, tying the fall of Egypt to the covenant history of Judah. The events are perfectly ordinary as history and perfectly governed as providence, and Scripture never treats those as competing explanations.

The death of Josiah at that hinge is the sober warning. Necho sent word that his quarrel was not with Judah and that God had bidden him make haste, and the chronicler records that Josiah “hearkened not unto the words of Necho from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo”. The best king since David, who had purged the land and kept the greatest Passover since Samuel, died because he would not hear a true word that came through an unwelcome mouth. Faithfulness in the past does not exempt a man from listening in the present.
roots_lines: Hebrew Karkemiysh (H3751) — Carchemish, a fortress on the Euphrates crossing.
Hebrew Perath (H6578) — the Euphrates; the river by which the empire changed hands.
Hebrew Nekow (H5224) — Necho, the Pharaoh whose warning Josiah refused.
Hebrew Nebuwkadretstsar (H5019) — Nebuchadrezzar, whom Jeremiah calls God's servant.
Hebrew Megiddow (H4023) — Megiddo, the valley where Josiah was shot.
usage: “Is not Calno as Carchemish?” — the Assyrian's boast.
“Necho king of Egypt came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates”.
“Which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon smote” — an empire ends at a ford.

pos: n. (proper, a prince of Babylon; Nergal, protect the king)
etymology: Babylonian Nergal-shar-usur, may Nergal protect the king — Nergal being the Babylonian god of war and pestilence. The name appears twice in Jeremiah 39, among the officers who sat in the middle gate of a conquered Jerusalem.
biblical_def: When the wall was breached the Babylonian staff took their seats where Jerusalem's elders had judged: “And all the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate, even Nergalsharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, with all the residue of the princes of the king of Babylon” (Jeremiah 39:3). The gate was the courthouse of a Hebrew city, and the men sitting in it now bear names invoking Nergal and Nebo. The same officer reappears in the party that fetches Jeremiah out of the court of the prison: “So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard sent, and Nebushasban, Rabsaris, and Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, and all the king of Babylon's princes” (Jeremiah 39:13). The prophet his own countrymen had put in a dungeon was treated well by the men whose gods he had preached against — Nebuchadrezzar had given charge concerning him, and they looked well to him and did him no harm.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of a prince of Babylon, styled Rab-mag, who sat in the middle gate at the taking of Jerusalem.
webster_full: BABYLON, n. The ancient capital of Chaldea, on the Euphrates; in Scripture, the type of the world in its pride and its fall.
GATE, n. The place of entrance into a walled city; among the Hebrews, the place where courts were held and public business transacted.
PRINCE, n. A sovereign; the chief and independent ruler of a nation; also, the chief officers of a king.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy by force or the fate of war.
MAGI, n. Wise men or philosophers of the East; a priestly and learned caste among the Chaldeans and Persians.
scriptures: Jeremiah 39:3

And all the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate, even Nergalsharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, with all the residue of the princes of the king of Babylon.
Jeremiah 39:13
So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard sent, and Nebushasban, Rabsaris, and Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, and all the king of Babylon's princes;
Jeremiah 39:12
Take him, and look well to him, and do him no harm; but do unto him even as he shall say unto thee.
Jeremiah 38:6

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.
corruption_summary: Faithful preaching is assumed to earn the goodwill of one's own people; Jeremiah was let down into the mire by the princes of Judah and lifted out by the princes of Babylon.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is one of the hardest in Scripture. Jeremiah 38 records that the princes of Judah cast the prophet into a dungeon where there was no water but mire, and he sank in the mire. Jeremiah 39 records that Nergal-sharezer and the officers of Babylon fetched him out and looked well to him. The men who feared Nergal and Nebo treated God's prophet better than the covenant community that had his own Scriptures. A servant of God has no promise that faithfulness will be rewarded by his own people, and the pattern runs to the cross.

The second thing is the middle gate itself. In a Hebrew city the gate was where the elders sat, causes were heard and judgments given. When Babylon took Jerusalem, her princes did not pull the gate down; they sat in it. A conqueror occupies the seat of judgment, and a people who have corrupted their own justice discover they have simply exchanged judges. Amos had warned Israel to establish judgment in the gate; a nation that will not do so does not keep its gate empty, it merely finds strangers in it.
roots_summary: Babylonian Nergal-shar-usur, Nergal protect the king; Hebrew Nergal Sharetser (H5371); Rab-mag (H7248), chief of the magi; shaar (H8179), a gate.
roots_lines: Hebrew Nergal Sharetser (H5371) — Nergal-sharezer; Babylonian for Nergal, protect the king.
Hebrew Nergal (H5370) — the Babylonian god of war and plague, named in 2 Kings 17:30.
Hebrew Rab-mag (H7248) — chief of the magi or soothsayers; his office in Jeremiah 39.
Hebrew shaar (H8179) — a gate; the seat of judgment in a Hebrew city.
Hebrew tiyt (H2916) — mire, clay; what Judah's own princes lowered Jeremiah into.
usage: “Came in, and sat in the middle gate” — strangers in the seat of judgment.
“Look well to him, and do him no harm” — the charge given about Jeremiah.
“Jeremiah sunk in the mire” — at the hands of his own countrymen.

etymology: An Egyptian royal name of uncertain meaning, borne by the queen in whose household an Edomite prince was raised. She is named three times in two verses of 1 Kings 11, and the detail matters more than its brevity suggests.
biblical_def: Hadad the Edomite fled to Egypt as a little child when Joab had spent six months burying every male in Edom. Pharaoh received him, and the connection deepened: “And Hadad found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him to wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen” (1 Kings 11:19). The next verse follows the child of that marriage into the royal nursery: “And the sister of Tahpenes bare him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house: and Genubath was in Pharaoh's household among the sons of Pharaoh” (1 Kings 11:20). The chapter is the account of God raising up adversaries against Solomon for his idolatry, and Hadad is the first of them. A queen of Egypt weaning an Edomite boy beside her own sons is the small domestic fact through which a kingdom's chastisement was prepared years in advance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of an Egyptian queen, sister-in-law to Hadad the Edomite and nurse of his son Genubath.
webster_full: QUEEN, n. The consort of a king; also, a woman who is the sovereign of a kingdom.
WEAN, v.t. To accustom and reconcile a child or other young animal to a want or deprivation of the breast.
ADVERSARY, n. An enemy or foe; one who has enmity at heart; an opponent or antagonist.
EDOM, n. The country and descendants of Esau, southeast of the Dead sea; a perpetual adversary of Israel.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
scriptures: 1 Kings 11:19
And Hadad found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him to wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.
1 Kings 11:20
And the sister of Tahpenes bare him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house: and Genubath was in Pharaoh's household among the sons of Pharaoh.
1 Kings 11:14
And the LORD stirred up an adversary unto Solomon, Hadad the Edomite: he was of the king's seed in Edom.
1 Kings 11:11

Wherefore the LORD said unto Solomon, Forasmuch as this is done of thee, and thou hast not kept my covenant and my statutes, which I have commanded thee, I will surely rend the kingdom from thee, and will give it to thy servant. is
corruption_summary: Chastening is imagined as a sudden stroke that arrives when sin is discovered; 1 Kings 11 shows God raising an adversary decades beforehand, in a nursery, while the offender was still at the height of his glory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the patience and precision of God's discipline. 1 Kings 11:14 says plainly, And the LORD stirred up an adversary unto Solomon, Hadad the Edomite — and then the narrative reaches back to a frightened child carried into Egypt long before Solomon's heart was turned away by his wives. The queen who weaned Genubath was not planning a war. God was. Nothing about the household arrangement was unusual, and every part of it was ordered.

The second observation is about the nursery itself. Genubath grew up in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh, and Hadad eventually asked leave to return to his own country with the words let me depart, that I may go to mine own country. A generation raised in a foreign court kept its memory and its grievance. Scripture repeatedly shows that what is formed in a household in one generation comes out in the politics of the next, and that God governs the weaning of children as surely as the raising of armies.
roots_lines: Hebrew Tachpeneyc (H8472) — Tahpenes, the Egyptian queen of 1 Kings 11.
Hebrew Hadad (H1908) — Hadad the Edomite, the adversary the LORD stirred up.
Hebrew Genubath (H1592) — theft; the name of the son weaned in Pharaoh's house.
Hebrew satan (H7854) — an adversary; the word used of Hadad against Solomon.
Hebrew gamal (H1580) — to deal out, to wean; whom Tahpenes weaned.
usage: “The sister of Tahpenes the queen” — a marriage in a foreign court.
“Whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house” — a nursery prepares a war.
“The LORD stirred up an adversary unto Solomon” — the stated cause.

pos: n. (proper, keeper of the women in Shushan)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning; spelled Hege at his first appearance and Hegai thereafter. He was the king's chamberlain over the house of the women in Shushan the palace, and his judgment of Esther is recorded with unusual care.
biblical_def: The plan to replace Vashti put every fair young virgin of the empire “unto the custody of Hege the king's chamberlain, keeper of the women” (Esther 2:3). When the decree was heard, “many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai”, and “Esther was brought also unto the king's house” (Esther 2:8). The text then records that she pleased him and obtained kindness of him, and he speedily gave her her things for purification with seven maidens and preferred her to the best place of the house of the women. The decisive verse comes at her turn: Esther “required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed” (Esther 2:15). Every other woman chose what she would take in to the king; the one who took only what the man who knew the king best advised is the one who obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the king of Persia's chamberlain, the keeper of the women in Shushan the palace.
webster_full: CHAMBERLAIN, n. An officer charged with the direction and management of a chamber, or of chambers; in Scripture, a eunuch of the royal household.
CUSTODY, n. A keeping; a guarding; care, watch, inspection, for keeping, preservation or security.
SHUSHAN, n. Susa, the winter capital of the Persian kings, the scene of the book of Esther.
COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct of another.
MODESTY, n. That lowly temper which accompanies a moderate estimate of one's own worth and importance.
scriptures: Esther 2:3

And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hege the king's chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given them: unto
Esther 2:8

So it came to pass, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king's house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women.
Esther 2:15

Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, was come to go in unto the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed. And Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her.
Esther 2:9

And the maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness of him; and he speedily gave her her things for purification, with such things as belonged to her, and seven maidens, which were meet to be given her, out of the king's house: and he preferred her and her maids unto the best place of the house of the women.
corruption_summary: Self-presentation is now taught as self-assertion — take what you want, present yourself as you choose — where Esther's favour is expressly tied to requiring nothing but what the keeper of the women appointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther 2:15 is written so as to make the contrast unmissable. Every maiden was entitled to take with her whatsoever she desired out of the house of the women. Esther required nothing but what Hegai the king's chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed, and the next clause reports the result: she obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her. In a culture that instructs young people to trust their own instinct about how to present themselves and to treat counsel as an infringement, Esther's restraint reads as weakness. Scripture records it as the hinge on which a nation's deliverance turned.

There is a second and more sober note, and honesty about the book requires it. Esther is not a manual for how to enter a pagan king's harem; the narrative is deliberately reticent and never commends the circumstances into which she was taken. What it displays is God's providence working through a situation his people had no power to refuse, and the wisdom of a young woman who took the counsel of a man who actually knew the court. The application is not to the palace but to the principle: the humble are guided in judgment, and God gives grace to the lowly.

pos: n. (proper, one of the seven princes of Persia and Media)
etymology: Persian, of uncertain meaning. He is named three times in Esther 1, as one of the seven princes “which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom” — and his advice set the whole book in motion.
biblical_def: The seven counsellors are listed by name: “Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom” (Esther 1:14). When a drunken king asked what should be done with a queen who would not come, Memucan answered, and he answered enormously: “Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus” (Esther 1:16). He proposed an irrevocable decree deposing her and a letter to every province. And the king took it: “the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan” (Esther 1:21). The whole book follows from that counsel — the throne left empty, the search for a new queen, Esther brought in, and a nation saved — none of which Memucan intended.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as one of the seven princes of Persia and Media whose counsel deposed Vashti.
webster_full: COUNSELLOR, n. Any person who gives advice; particularly, one whose profession is to give advice in law or in affairs of state.
DECREE, n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an edict or law made by a superior as a rule to govern inferiors.
PERSIA, n. A great kingdom of western Asia, which succeeded Babylon in the empire of the East.
MEDIA, n. An ancient country of Asia, joined with Persia in the empire of Cyrus and his successors.
OVERRULE, v.t. To control by superior power or authority; to govern with high authority.
scriptures: Esther 1:14
And the next unto him was Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king's face, and which sat the first in the kingdom;)
Esther 1:16

And Memucan answered before the king and the princes, Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus.
Esther 1:21
And the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan:
Esther 1:19

If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she. If
corruption_summary: Policy made in anger and passed in haste is presented as decisive leadership; Memucan's counsel was given to a drunken king, made irrevocable by law, and used by God for the opposite of what he intended.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther 1 is a study in how bad government is made. The king is merry with wine, publicly humiliated, and furious; his advisers are at hand; and within a few verses an empire-wide decree has been issued that cannot be reversed, because the law of the Persians and the Medes altereth not. Memucan's speech even inflates the offence — not wrong to the king only, but to all the princes and all the people in all the provinces. Counsel given to flatter a ruler's wounded pride, dressed as concern for the public order, is among the oldest species of political folly, and Scripture puts it on record without comment.

The comment is supplied by what follows. The vacancy Memucan created is the door through which Esther entered, and the God who is never once named in this book governed every step of it. Proverbs says the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will. That is exactly what Esther 1 shows. Men make decrees in anger, and the decrees hold; and the purpose they serve is not the one the counsellor had in mind when he stood up to speak.

Hebrew Achashverowsh (H325) — Ahasuerus, the king whose heart God turned.
Hebrew Vashtiy (H2060) — Vashti, the queen deposed by Memucan's counsel.

“The king did according to the word of Memucan” — and the book begins.
“That it be not altered” — a decree made irrevocable in anger.

pos: n. (proper, a Roman emperor; also a chief captain in Jerusalem)
etymology: Latin Claudius, a Roman family name. The Authorized Version uses it of two men: Claudius Caesar, the fourth emperor, and Claudius Lysias, the chief captain whose letter sent Paul to Caesarea.
biblical_def: Agabus came down to Antioch and “signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar” (Acts 11:28) — and the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief to the brethren in Judaea. The emperor appears again as the cause of a providential meeting: at Corinth Paul “found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:)” (Acts 18:2). An imperial expulsion order put the apostle in a tentmaker's house. The second Claudius is the officer who rescued Paul from the mob and later from an ambush, and whose letter is quoted verbatim: “Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting” (Acts 23:26). Roman law, Roman roads and Roman edicts all serve the spread of the gospel in Acts without intending to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the Roman emperor in whose days the great dearth came, and of the chief captain Claudius Lysias.
webster_full: CAESAR, n. A title of the Roman emperors, derived from the family name of Julius Caesar.
DEARTH, n. Scarcity; such a want of any thing as renders it dear; particularly, a scarcity of food.
EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince.
CHIEF CAPTAIN, n. In the New Testament, the tribune commanding a Roman cohort, as Claudius Lysias at Jerusalem.
CITIZENSHIP, n. The state of being vested with the rights and privileges of a citizen.
scriptures: Acts 11:28
And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar.
Acts 18:2
And found a certain Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, lately come from Italy, with his wife Priscilla; (because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome:) and came unto them.
Acts 23:26
Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting.
Acts 11:29
Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea:
corruption_summary: The state is treated either as the church's enemy to be defied or as her patron to be courted; Acts shows an emperor's expulsion order and a tribune's letter serving the gospel without either man intending it.
corruption_paragraphs: Two settled attitudes toward civil power crowd out the biblical one. The first treats the magistrate as simply hostile, so that every edict is persecution and every officer an enemy. The second courts the state for favour and shapes the church's message to keep it. Acts 18:2 will not fit either. Claudius commanded all Jews to depart from Rome — an unjust order that uprooted households — and the immediate result in the text is that Paul found Aquila and Priscilla, worked at tents with them, and gained two of the most useful colleagues in the New Testament. God's providence is not obstructed by an unjust decree; it runs through it.

Claudius Lysias fills out the picture from the other side. He bound Paul to examine him by scourging, released him when he learned he was a Roman, rescued him from forty men under an oath to kill him, and wrote a self-serving letter that quietly improved his own conduct in the telling. Paul used the protection, appealed to his citizenship, and was carried to Rome by the very system that had chained him. The believer's duty is to honour the magistrate, to use lawful protection without shame, and to obey God rather than men where the two conflict — and to expect God to reach his ends through officials who are serving their own.
roots_summary: Greek Klaudios (G2804), Claudius; limos (G3042), a famine or dearth; chiliarchos (G5506), a chief captain; diatasso (G1299), to command or ordain.
roots_lines: Greek Klaudios (G2804) — Claudius; used of the emperor and of Claudius Lysias.
Greek limos (G3042) — famine, dearth; the scarcity Agabus foretold by the Spirit.
Greek chiliarchos (G5506) — a commander of a thousand, a chief captain; Lysias's rank.
Greek diatasso (G1299) — to arrange, to command; Claudius commanded the Jews to depart.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, relief; what the disciples sent to Judaea in the dearth.
usage: “Which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar” — a prophecy dated.
“Because that Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome”.
“Claudius Lysias unto the most excellent governor Felix sendeth greeting”.

pos: n. (proper, a king of Mesopotamia; Cushan of double wickedness)
etymology: Hebrew Kuwshan Rishathayim — Cushan with the dual ending of rishah, wickedness: Cushan of double wickedness. He is the first oppressor in the book of Judges, and the first deliverance in that book is from him.
biblical_def: The pattern of Judges is set by this king. “Therefore the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years” (Judges 3:8). Note who sold them: not a failure of Israel's defences but the anger of the LORD, and the oppressor is the instrument. Then the cry, and then the deliverer — Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother: “And the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war: and the LORD delivered Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand; and his hand prevailed against Chushanrishathaim” (Judges 3:10). Four elements appear here that will repeat through the book: Israel does evil, God sells them, Israel cries, God raises a deliverer on whom his Spirit comes. The name itself — double wickedness — is the sort of thing Hebrew narrative enjoys, and the land had rest forty years.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the king of Mesopotamia who oppressed Israel eight years and was delivered into the hand of Othniel.
webster_full: MESOPOTAMIA, n. The country between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates; in Hebrew, Aram-naharaim, Syria of the two rivers.
OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity or rigor.
DELIVERER, n. One who delivers; one who releases or rescues; a preserver.
JUDGE, n. In the Hebrew commonwealth, a chief magistrate raised up by God to deliver and govern Israel.
CHASTISE, v.t. To correct by punishment; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender.
scriptures: Judges 3:8
Therefore the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years.
Judges 3:10

And the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war: and the LORD delivered Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand; and his hand prevailed against Chushanrishathaim.
Judges 3:9
And when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.
Judges 3:11
And the land had rest forty years. And Othniel the son of Kenaz died.
corruption_summary: Oppression is explained wholly by the strength and malice of the oppressor, where Judges 3 says the LORD sold Israel into his hand — and that the same LORD delivered him into Othniel's.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 3:8 states a cause that no modern analysis would supply: the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them. The oppressor was real, his power was real, and eight years of servitude were real; and the text puts the transaction in God's hands. This is not a denial that Chushan-rishathaim was wicked — his very name in the record is doubled wickedness — nor an excuse for him, since God judged him too. It is the refusal of a purely horizontal account of history. A nation that will not consider whether God is chastening it will learn nothing from its troubles.

The deliverance is described with equal care. Israel cried unto the LORD, and the LORD raised up a deliverer, and the Spirit of the LORD came upon him. Othniel did not volunteer, and his qualification is not his ability but the Spirit. The pattern holds through the book and through redemptive history: the people cry, God provides a deliverer of his own choosing and equipping, and the land has rest. Judges is the Old Testament's long argument that men cannot save themselves, told seven times over, and pointing beyond every judge to one Deliverer on whom the Spirit rested without measure.
roots_summary: Hebrew Kuwshan Rishathayim (H3573), Cushan of double wickedness; Aram Naharayim (H763), Mesopotamia; makar (H4376), to sell; Othniyel (H6274), Othniel.
roots_lines: Hebrew Kuwshan Rishathayim (H3573) — Chushan-rishathaim; Cushan of double wickedness.
Hebrew rishah (H7564) — wickedness; doubled in the oppressor's very name.
Hebrew Aram Naharayim (H763) — Syria of the two rivers, Mesopotamia; his kingdom.
Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; the LORD sold Israel into his hand.
Hebrew Othniyel (H6274) — Othniel, lion of God; the first judge, Caleb's younger brother.
usage: “He sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim” — the stated cause.
“The Spirit of the LORD came upon him” — the deliverer's qualification.
“And the land had rest forty years” — the pattern completed.

pos: n. (proper, a Canaanite king; lord of Bezek)
etymology: Hebrew Adoniy-Bezeq, lord of Bezek. He appears in the first chapter of Judges, and pronounces upon himself one of the plainest statements of retributive justice in Scripture.
biblical_def: Judah went up against the Canaanites and “found Adonibezek in Bezek: and they fought against him, and they slew the Canaanites and the Perizzites” (Judges 1:5). “But Adonibezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes” (Judges 1:6) — a mutilation that disabled a man from holding a sword or standing to fight. Then the king himself supplies the commentary: “Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me. And they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died” (Judges 1:7). He had done the same to seventy kings and fed them like dogs beneath his table. He does not plead, excuse, or accuse his captors of cruelty. He names his own deeds, names God as the one requiting, and dies.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the title of a Canaanite king of Bezek, who confessed that God had requited him as he had done to others.
webster_full: REQUITE, v.t. To repay; to recompense; to return an equivalent in good or evil.
RETRIBUTION, n. Repayment; return accommodated to the action; reward or punishment suitably bestowed.
MUTILATE, v.t. To cut off a limb or essential part of an animal body; to maim.
CANAANITE, n. A descendant of Canaan, the son of Ham; one of the nations dispossessed by Israel.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong; the faculty by which we judge the moral quality of our own actions.
scriptures: Judges 1:5
And they found Adonibezek in Bezek: and they fought against him, and they slew the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
Judges 1:6
But Adonibezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes.
Judges 1:7

And Adonibezek said, Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me. And they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died. their
Galatians 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
corruption_summary: Retributive justice is widely dismissed as primitive vengeance dressed up, and yet the clearest statement of it in Scripture comes from the mouth of the man it fell on, who did not dispute it.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern thought treats retribution as the least defensible part of justice: punishment should deter, reform or protect, but the idea that a man should simply be repaid for what he did is written off as cruelty with a theory. Judges 1:7 is remarkable because the sentence is pronounced by the criminal. As I have done, so God hath requited me. Adoni-bezek does not protest that his captors were no better, or that his upbringing explains the seventy kings under his table. He recognizes a proportion between his deeds and his end, and he names the God of Israel as the one who kept the account, though he had never worshipped him.

Paul states the same law for every man in Galatians 6:7 — be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. The reason Christians can look steadily at Judges 1 is not that the justice there is softened but that it has been satisfied elsewhere. The gospel does not abolish requital; it announces that Christ bore it. A man is repaid either in himself or in his Substitute, and the horror of Adoni-bezek's confession is precisely what makes the cross intelligible.
roots_summary: Hebrew Adoniy-Bezeq (H137), lord of Bezek; shalam (H7999), to requite or make whole; bohen (H931), a thumb or great toe; Yehuwdah (H3063), Judah.
roots_lines: Hebrew Adoniy-Bezeq (H137) — Adoni-bezek, lord of Bezek; a title rather than a personal name.
Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to make whole, to repay, to requite; so God hath requited me.
Hebrew bohen (H931) — a thumb or great toe; the mutilation he inflicted and received.
Hebrew Bezeq (H966) — Bezek, lightning; the place of his rule and his defeat.
Greek mukterizo (G3456) — to turn up the nose, to mock; God is not mocked.
usage: “Threescore and ten kings... gathered their meat under my table”.
“As I have done, so God hath requited me” — the criminal's own verdict.
“Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” — the same law.

pos: n. (proper, a priest of Baal; Hebrew, a gift)
etymology: Hebrew Mattan, a gift — from nathan, to give. The irony is unmissable: the priest of Baal slain before his own altars bore a name meaning gift, and Scripture names a second Mattan, father of one of Jeremiah's persecutors.
biblical_def: When Jehoiada the priest brought the boy Joash out of hiding and crowned him, the covenant renewal did not stop at the palace: “And all the people of the land went into the house of Baal, and brake it down; his altars and his images brake they in pieces thoroughly, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars” (2 Kings 11:18). The chronicler records the same act in the same terms (2 Chronicles 23:17). Athaliah's six-year reign had installed a rival worship with its own house, its own images and its own priesthood, and a reformation that had left the house of Baal standing would have been no reformation. A second Mattan appears in Jeremiah's day as the father of Shephatiah, one of the princes who heard Jeremiah's words and demanded his death (Jeremiah 38:1) — the men who then put the prophet in the miry dungeon.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the name of the priest of Baal slain before the altars in the reformation under Jehoiada.
webster_full: BAAL, n. The chief male deity of the Phoenicians and Canaanites; a name signifying lord or master.
REFORMATION, n. Change from worse to better; amendment of life; the great religious revolution of the sixteenth century.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; an idol.
COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons; in Scripture, God's gracious engagement with his people.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or any thing made by hands, or which is not God.
scriptures: 2 Kings 11:18

And all the people of the land went into the house of Baal, and brake it down; his altars and his images brake they in pieces thoroughly, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars. And the priest appointed officers over the house of the LORD.
2 Chronicles 23:17
Then all the people went to the house of Baal, and brake it down, and brake his altars and his images in pieces, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars.
Jeremiah 38:1

Then Shephatiah the son of Mattan, and Gedaliah the son of Pashur, and Jucal the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah, heard the words that Jeremiah had spoken unto all the people, saying,
2 Kings 11:17
And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, that they should be the LORD'S people; between the king also and the people.
corruption_summary: Reformation is imagined as a change of personal conviction that leaves rival institutions standing; under Jehoiada the covenant was renewed and the house of Baal was broken down the same day.
corruption_paragraphs: The reformation under Jehoiada has a shape that later reformers recognized. First a covenant — between the LORD and the king and the people, that they should be the LORD'S people — and then, immediately, the house of Baal broken down, the altars and images broken thoroughly, and the priest of Baal slain before the altars. Nothing was left standing to be returned to. A repentance that renews vows while carefully preserving the machinery of the old idolatry has not repented; Scripture's pattern is that the high places come down, and Judah's kings are judged, one after another, by whether they did.

Two cautions belong here. The first is that the civil sword used in 2 Kings 11 was Israel's under a theocratic covenant, not the church's in this age; our weapons are not carnal, and idols today are broken by preaching, discipline and repentance rather than by execution. The second is the name. Mattan means gift, and the second Mattan in Scripture fathered a man who sought a prophet's life. A good name, a respectable office and a religious vocabulary are no evidence at all of which side of a reformation a man will be found on.
roots_summary: Hebrew Mattan (H4977), a gift; nathan (H5414), to give; Baal (H1168), lord; mizbeach (H4196), an altar.
roots_lines: Hebrew Mattan (H4977) — a gift; the name of the priest of Baal slain before the altars.
Hebrew nathan (H5414) — to give; the root of Mattan, Nathan, Mattaniah and Jonathan.
Hebrew Baal (H1168) — lord, master; the Canaanite deity Athaliah had established in Judah.
Hebrew mizbeach (H4196) — an altar, a place of slaughter; where his own end came.
Hebrew beriyth (H1285) — a covenant; renewed by Jehoiada before the house of Baal fell.
usage: “Slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars” — nothing left standing.
“Brake his altars and his images in pieces” — thoroughly, says the text.
“Shephatiah the son of Mattan” — a good name on a bad side.
